title: How heavy can a dead star be?
blurb: A young physicist from Madras, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, worked out that a white dwarf star cannot be more than about 1.4 times as heavy as the Sun.

original.title: The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs

cards.b: A star like our Sun shines by using up fuel at her centre. When the fuel runs out, the star collapses into a small, very dense star called a white dwarf. Inside, tiny particles called electrons are packed tightly together and push against being squeezed. That push holds the star up. But can it hold up a star of any weight, however heavy?

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore in 1910 and grew up in Madras, now Chennai. He studied physics at Presidency College in Madras. In 1930 he went to the University of Cambridge in England. In 1931, while still in his early twenties, he published papers on white dwarf stars.

img.alt: A drawing of NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory in space, which was named after Chandrasekhar

cards.b: Chandrasekhar did not use a telescope. He used maths and two big ideas of physics. Relativity explains how things behave when they move very fast. Quantum mechanics explains how very tiny things, like electrons, behave. Putting the two together, he worked out how the electrons' push changes as a white dwarf gets heavier.

The electrons' push has a limit. Mass is how much stuff something is made of. If a white dwarf has more than about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, the push cannot hold it up, and it collapses. This is now called the Chandrasekhar limit. So stars much heavier than the Sun cannot end as white dwarfs. They must end another way, by exploding or becoming black holes.

Today the limit is basic to much of astronomy. But at first, people argued about it. In January 1935, the famous astronomer Arthur Eddington strongly disagreed with Chandrasekhar. Some questions are still open. Astronomers believe a white dwarf pushed past the limit blows up, but what pushes it over is still a mystery.

A supernova is a huge explosion of a star. A white dwarf pushed past the limit blows up as a kind called Type Ia. These explosions shine with a brightness astronomers can predict, so they use them to measure how fast the universe is growing. That led to the discovery of dark energy. In 1983 Chandrasekhar shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on how stars are built and change.

img.alt: The glowing remains of a Type Ia supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, photographed by Hubble
img.credit: NASA, ESA (Hubble Space Telescope), public domain

cards.b: Feel packed things push back. Fill a steel tumbler loosely with cotton wool and press it down with your palm. At first it squashes easily. As it packs tighter, it pushes back harder. Your palm is like the star's own weight pressing in. In a white dwarf, the packed electrons push back and hold the star up. Past about 1.4 Suns, even that push is not enough.

Chandrasekhar was in his twenties when a famous older scientist argued against his idea. Today his limit is used everywhere in astronomy. When an expert disagrees with you, how do you decide whether to change your mind or keep going? What would help you check?
